source: Cemri et al. (2025) Denario project: Deep knowledge AI agents for scientific discovery, section 7.2
finding: The only 2025-2026 AI paper found that invokes Lakatos in the AI-science setting. It asks whether an LLM-driven programme can be progressive without a human-readable theoretical core. It gives no measurement and no trace labelling.
quote: a progressive programme predicts novel facts and accommodates anomalies, while a degenerative one merely accommodates data retrospectively
limits: Essay-level discussion. Does not label agent traces or test any stopping rule. Author attribution of the Denario paper not checked.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 stays open: Lakatos is cited as philosophy, not operationalised. Our operational test (K02) would be new.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Understanding the Dark Side of LLMs' Intrinsic Self-Correction (v2, Jul 2025)
finding: Intrinsic self-correction with no oracle still lowers accuracy in 2025 models, including o1-preview, o1-mini and 4o on Yes/No questions, and ChatGPT models on HotpotQA, HumanEval and AlfWorld. Text: accuracy falls after feedback and refinement in all four tasks. DeepSeek V3 and R1 were also tested on Yes/No questions.
numbers: Appendix B Yes/No rows: o1-preview 74.1 accuracy after refinement (4.2 points lower), 15.6% of correct answers overturned; o1-mini 62.5 (12.1 lower), 34.0% overturned; 4o 49.2 (20.4 lower), 58.8% overturned; 3.5-turbo 52.8 (8.7 lower), 26.5%. Tasks: AlfWorld 134 environments, HotpotQA 100 questions, HumanEval 161 functions.
quote: intrinsic self-correction fails without oracle labels as feedback
limits: pdftotext table layout dropped some row labels, so DeepSeek, Llama and complex-task rows could not be matched to models with certainty and are not quoted. Prompt follows Huang: refine regardless of whether the first answer was right.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: the Huang no-oracle result still holds for reasoning models in 2025, with smaller drops for o1-preview than for 4o. No equal-token comparison is made. Do not revise on an unverified signal.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Dark Side of Intrinsic Self-Correction, interpretation and alleviation sections
finding: Why it fails. On simple questions the model wavers in intermediate and final answers. On decision tasks failures look like human biases. Repeating the original question at the end of the refinement prompt reduces the damage.
numbers: GPT-3.5-turbo changes 81.3% of answers more than 6 times in 10 rounds (text). Llama internal answer changes 14.1% of the time after the 'are you sure' prompt vs 8.3% at first answer. Failure split in decision making: perfectionism bias 49.0%, cognitive overload 33.3%, overthinking 17.6%. Question repeating raises accuracy 3.2-4.9 points and cuts overturned answers 5.3-10.9 points; SFT on few samples also helps.
limits: Mechanistic part only on open Llama. Failure split is from AlfWorld logs only. Snapshot dated 2025-02-15.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 (partly): a prompt that re-anchors the original task (our S1 restatement) reduced drift in one study. This is not a test of repeated patches.

source: Stroebl, Kapoor, Narayanan (2024-2026) The Limits of Inference Scaling Through Resampling (v3 Mar 2026)
finding: A check with a non-zero false positive rate caps what retrying can reach. Weak models have more false positives, and the false positive rate rises with the number of attempts K. With a cost for false positives the best K is finite and small.
numbers: HumanEval+ 200 samples per task (1000 for Command Light), MBPP+ 50 per task. At cost-benefit ratio 4 the optimal K is about 5 for all four models. Ratios tried: 0, 1, 2, 4, 8. At high enough ratio the best K is zero.
quote: the optimal number of samples is finite and low
limits: Verifier is the weak original unit tests, not an LLM judge. Authors say LLM-generated tests are an open question. Llama-3.1-70B false positive rate rises sharply with K, Code Llama and Command rise slowly; no explanation given.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: gives a worked break-even form: attempt only while expected benefit of a true pass exceeds false-pass cost times false-positive rate. S0 can estimate the check's false positive rate on a few items and set the cap K from it.

source: Snell et al. (2024) Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters
finding: Sequential revision (fine-tuned revision model) narrowly beats the same number of parallel samples. There is a compute-optimal ratio of sequential to parallel that depends on question difficulty. Easy questions favour sequential refinement; hard ones favour parallel search.
numbers: MATH, PaLM 2-S. About 38% of correct answers get changed to incorrect by the naive revision model. Revision model trained on up to 4 prior answers; pass@1 kept rising beyond 4 revision steps. Beam search hurt on easy bins as budget grew (over-optimised the verifier).
limits: Revision model is fine-tuned, so this is not prompt-only revision. Verifier is a trained PRM. Single model family. Difficulty-split direction taken from the paper's summary text.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 (exact vs open): difficulty decides patching vs restarting. A hard problem should switch to a fresh attempt sooner; an easy one should patch. Supports an S0 difficulty estimate feeding the S6 threshold. The 38% flip rate is a base rate for how often a patch destroys a right answer.

source: Chen, Lin, Scharli, Zhou (2023) Teaching Large Language Models to Self-Debug
finding: With execution feedback, most of the gain comes from the first debugging turn. The turn cap was 10 but successful debugging mostly ended within 3 turns.
numbers: TransCoder: one debugging turn with full feedback gives about +12 points over greedy. Spider: debugging from greedy matches the 16-sample baseline; from 8 samples beats the 32-sample baseline. Max turns 10, successes mostly within 3.
limits: Execution feedback and unit tests are external signals. Text on Spider extra turns is ambiguously worded.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: the 'mostly within 3 turns' pattern is a data point for a cap of 2-3 failed patches when the check is real.

source: Gou et al. (2024) CRITIC: LLMs Can Self-Correct With Tool-Interactive Critiquing
finding: Iterative correction with tool feedback improves, but gains shrink fast. Without reliable feedback, self-improvement is poor and inefficient.
numbers: Authors: 2-3 rounds of correction give most of the benefit; the oracle setting (only editing wrong samples) gives a notable surge. ChatGPT, Figures 3-5.
quote: 2-3 rounds of corrections yield most of the benefits
limits: Numbers are in figures, not read. Statement taken from the analysis text.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 and gap 4: again 2-3 rounds, and the oracle gap shows the value of knowing which items are wrong, which is the check-reliability point.

source: Li et al. (2025) S*: Test Time Scaling for Code Generation
finding: Ablation of iterative debugging. Benefit plateaus after 2-3 rounds. Debugging on model-generated tests did not help over public tests only, because wrong generated outputs add noise. Keeping only the last round as context helped one model and hurt two.
numbers: QwQ-32B-Preview 72.6 to 74.2 with 2 debugging rounds. Up to 4 rounds tested. Reasoning models still gained from explicit execution feedback even though they reflect internally.
quote: The benefits of iterative debugging tend to plateau, typically after 2-3 rounds
limits: LiveCodeBench; three models; small gains. Context result is mixed (Qwen2.5-Coder-7B up, two others down).
agent_relevance: Gap 2: a self-made test (model-generated tests) did not separate good patches from bad; a real external test did. Gap 9: pruning history to the last attempt is not reliably better.

source: Cemri et al. (2025) Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail? (MAST)
finding: Taxonomy of 14 failure modes from 1600+ annotated multi-agent traces. Loop-related modes are common: step repetition and not recognising that the task is done. Verification gaps are a separate class.
numbers: Step repetition 15.7%; unaware of termination conditions 12.4%; premature termination 6.20%; no or incomplete verification 8.20%. Annotation kappa 0.88 on 150 expert traces, 0.77 for the LLM annotator. Adding a high-level task objective verification step to ChatDev gave +15.6% task success on ProgramDev.
limits: Multi-agent frameworks, not single-agent patch loops. Percentages are shares of annotated failures, not rates over all runs.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 and gap 8: step repetition is a measurable trace label, so a repeat-detector at S6 has a base rate. Both failure to stop (12.4%) and stopping early (6.2%) occur, so one rule must guard both.

source: Laban et al. (2025) LLMs Get Lost in Multi-Turn Conversation
finding: Models that take a wrong turn rarely recover. They lean on their own earlier incorrect answer attempts, answer too early, and bloat answers.
numbers: Average drop of 39% across six generation tasks from single-turn to multi-turn; 200,000+ simulated conversations. Aptitude loss about 15%, unreliability up 112% (figure labels).
quote: rely too heavily on previous (incorrect) answer attempts
limits: Underspecified-instruction sharding, not patching loops. Chat setting.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: supports starting a fresh attempt from the fixed task statement rather than editing a conversation full of failed attempts. Indirect, not a patch experiment.

source: Illusion of Diminishing Returns: Measuring Long Horizon Execution in LLMs (ICLR 2026)
finding: Models condition on their own earlier errors: per-step accuracy falls as the error rate in the history rises, beyond the effect of context length. Larger models are not spared. The paper says recent thinking models are not affected.
numbers: Counterfactual test: history injected with controlled error rates; accuracy at a fixed later turn drops as history error rate rises. Qwen3-32B accuracy falls below 50% at long horizon (Fig 4).
quote: models become more likely to make mistakes when the context contains their errors
limits: Synthetic long-horizon execution task, not repair. The thinking-model claim is from the summary text only. Authors not checked.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: keeping failed patches in context harms non-thinking models. Gap 3: reasoning models differ, so test the S6 rule separately on thinking and non-thinking backbones.

source: Liu et al. (2025) Understanding R1-Zero-Like Training: A Critical Perspective (COLM 2025)
finding: The 'aha moment' of self-reflection already appears in base models, and more self-reflection in R1-Zero does not go with higher accuracy.
numbers: DeepSeek-V3-Base-685B on 500 MATH questions with the R1 template generates self-reflection keywords ('aha', 'wait'). In R1-Zero, self-reflection behaviours are not positively correlated with accuracy.
quote: these behaviors are not positively correlated with higher accuracy
limits: Keyword counting as proxy for reflection. MATH only.
agent_relevance: Gap 3/8: more visible reflection is not evidence of useful revision; do not count 'wait'-style tokens as progress.

source: Muennighoff et al. (2025) s1: Simple test-time scaling
finding: Forcing more thinking by appending 'Wait' gives modest gains on a hard set and none on an easy one. Rejection sampling for short traces shows inverse scaling.
numbers: s1-32B AIME24: no extrapolation 50.0; 2x 'Wait' 53.3; 4x 56.7 (abstract: 50% to 57%). MATH500 93.0 at 2x, 92.2 at 4x. s1.1 AIME24 stays 56.7 at 1x and 2x.
limits: Table columns read from layout text. AIME24 has 30 problems, so one problem is 3.3 points; gains of 3-7 points are 1-2 problems.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: a floor on effort helps only on hard items; a fixed floor wastes tokens on easy ones. Supports a difficulty-gated floor.

source: Ghosal et al. (2025) Does Thinking More Always Help? Mirage of Test-Time Scaling in Reasoning Models
finding: Accuracy first rises then falls as thinking is extended with 'Wait'. A simple model says extra thinking raises output variance. Spending the same budget on parallel samples with majority vote does better.
numbers: GSM8K, R1-Distill model (Fig 2a): accuracy 82.2 to 87.3 as average thinking tokens go 385 to 1100, then 87.3 to 70.3 at 15,980 tokens. Entropy 0.23 to 2.79 (12x) as tokens go 385 to 6136. Parallel thinking up to 20% higher accuracy than extended thinking at equal budget.
quote: a critical point in the length of the thinking trace beyond which performance declines
agent_relevance: Gap 8 and gap 3: a stop rule is needed on both sides, a floor and a ceiling, and equal-token parallel sampling is a strong alternative to deeper patching.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Reasoning Models Know When They're Right: Probing Hidden States for Self-Verification
finding: A small probe on hidden states predicts whether an intermediate answer is correct, with good calibration. Using it to exit reasoning early cut tokens without losing accuracy.
numbers: In-distribution ROC-AUC above 0.7 and ECE below 0.1 for all probes; R1-Distill-Qwen-32B over 0.9 ROC-AUC on AIME. Early exit: 24% fewer inference tokens, accuracy unchanged. Out-of-distribution on AIME was weaker.
limits: Needs hidden-state access and training data; not available to a prompt-only scaffold on a closed model.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 and gap 8: shows a cheap calibrated correctness signal can drive stopping. For us the analogue is a measured check reliability estimated in S0, not hidden states.

source: Negative search record for gaps 6 and 10 (this session)
finding: One web search for Lakatos progressive/degenerating applied to LLM agent traces returned Denario (d01), Branahl on stagnant programmes (no LLM content), GraphTracer (failure tracing, no Lakatos in the snippet), and a non-arXiv preprint on governed inquiry. None labels traces. Meehl 1990 primary PDF returned HTTP 403 from meehl.umn.edu. arXiv, Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex search APIs were rate-limited, and later searches were refused for budget.
numbers: 0 studies found labelling traces progressive or degenerating. 1 search used for this gap.
limits: Absence of evidence under tool limits, not proof. GraphTracer and the preprints.org item were not opened.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 and gap 10 stay open. Treat the Lakatos mapping as our own design hypothesis.
